newsitem.title: GERMANY: German bank sector talks over sick pay adjourned.
newsitem.headline: German bank sector talks over sick pay adjourned.

text.p: Talks between Germany's banking employers and the main trade unions in the sector over sick pay made some progress on Wednesday but ended without a conclusive agreement, a spokesman for the Federation of Banking Employers said.

The spokesman said the two sides, which agreed to meet again on February 10, had narrowed their differences and had tackled thorny issues of continued payment of full sick pay and possible labour cost reductions.

Horst Mueller, chief negotiator for the Federation of Banking Employers had said earlier that if trade unions continued to insist on sick pay entitlements at 100 percent of salary, it would demand compensating reductions in other areas of labour costs.

The second round of talks follows an earlier meeting between employers and the DAG and HBV unions in December at which employers agreed to continue to pay full sick pay until a wider contractual agreeement was reached in the sector.

Germany's banks had earlier implemented a new law introduced last October allowing them to cut sick pay to 80 percent of salary but met with strong resistance from employees, some 15,000 of whom took part in a day of walk-outs and protests.
Mueller said before the talks started that the negotiators would aim to produce new employee contracts "that can lead us into the year 2000.

"It is no longer in accord with the times that a bank employee can earn more money simply because he sits in his chair and gets older," Mueller, also a board member of Dresdner Bank AG, Germany's second largest bank, said.
A spokesman for the HBV banking and insurance union said that it was looking for a 1997 pay rise of between 3.6 and 3.8 percent.

Germany's daily Germany's Bild newspaper, meanwhile, quoting a study by the German Association of Public Health Insurers, said the controversial sick-pay law has resulted in a drop of about 20 percent in the number of days claimed by employees.
Hans-Peter Stihl, president of the German Chambers of Industry and Commerce (DIHT), told the newspaper the new law had so far saved employers about 20 billion marks.
"This is the first sign that the reduction in the sick-pay laws have taken hold despite the difficulties," Stihl said.
